env_1.stem: Which action helps protect the environment?
options: Sorting at home, then dumping everything into one public bin
Using less paper but throwing all plastic in regular trash
Recycling paper, plastic, and glass in the right bins
Crushing bottles to save space without recycling them
env_1.explanation: Recycling reduces waste, saves raw materials, and helps protect the environment.
theoryLines: Protecting the environment includes reducing waste, recycling, and saving resources.
Recycling lets useful materials be made into new products.

options: A collection of human buildings with no living nature
Living things together with their surroundings and the links between them
Only museum samples with no living environment
A city building diagram with no plants, animals, or food links
env_2.explanation: An ecosystem includes living things, their habitat, and how they interact—for food, shelter, and more.
theoryLines: Examples include a forest, a pond, and a coral reef.
A change in the environment can affect every part of the ecosystem.

env_3.stem: Which statement about air pollution is true?
options: Air pollution can also affect human health
Air pollution affects only plants
Air pollution is not related to health
Only polluted water usually harms people
env_3.explanation: Air pollution can harm the lungs and lead to other health problems.
theoryLines: Common sources include traffic, industry, and burning fuels.
Reducing air pollution helps people and nature.

env_4.stem: Which statement about greenhouse gases is true?
options: They are rare in nature and do not affect Earth's warmth at all
They trap heat in the atmosphere, and their amount affects climate
They gather only above countries with tall mountains
They come mainly from volcanoes with no link to people
env_4.explanation: Gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat. Too much of them warms the planet.
theoryLines: A natural greenhouse effect helps keep Earth warm enough for life.
Human activity has added large amounts of greenhouse gases to the air.

env_5.stem: What is the best way to deal with used materials to protect the environment?
options: Throw everything in the trash without sorting it.
Always buy brand-new materials instead of reusing old ones.
Reduce, reuse, or send materials to recycling.
Burn all waste materials at home to get rid of them.
env_5.explanation: Reducing, reusing, and recycling materials helps protect the environment by creating less waste and saving natural resources.
theoryLines: Reducing how much we use is the most effective way to help the environment.
Recycling saves resources and helps reduce pollution.

env_6.stem: What helps keep the environment clean?
options: Cleaning only your house and leaving shared streets as they are
Putting trash in a bin instead of throwing it on the street
Collecting bottles in the yard and delaying pickup until spring
Packing trash until the bag tears before putting it in a bin
env_6.explanation: Putting trash in a bin—not on the street—helps keep places clean and pleasant.
theoryLines: Everyone can help keep the environment clean.
A cleaner environment is healthier and nicer for people.

options: In a trash bin or the right recycling container
Anywhere outdoors
Buried anywhere in the ground
Only into water
env_7.explanation: Trash belongs in a bin so the environment stays clean.
theoryLines: Trash bins are meant for collecting waste.
Using bins helps keep places clean and pleasant.

options: Burying everything in backyard soil with no sorting
Using old materials again to make new products
Piling waste forever in one place with no recycling
Crushing mixed materials together with no prep for reuse
env_8.explanation: Recycling turns used materials such as plastic, paper, and glass into new products instead of throwing them away.
theoryLines: Recycling helps protect the environment.
It reduces waste and saves resources.

options: An environment that is completely free of harmful materials
Adding harmful materials to the environment that cause damage
Rain that always washes every pollutant out of the air
Sunlight that fully blocks gases from entering the atmosphere
env_9.explanation: Pollution means harmful materials in air, water, or soil that can hurt animals, plants, and people.
theoryLines: Pollution can come from chimneys, cars, or trash.
It can harm nature and human health.

options: Developing wild land without checking effects on local species
Protecting nature, animals, and plants
Collecting litter outdoors only for display, not for recycling
Assuming nature always recovers by itself in a few days
env_10.explanation: Conservation means protecting nature so future generations can enjoy healthy plants, animals, and places.
theoryLines: Parks and nature reserves help protect habitats.
Everyone can help with conservation.

env_11.stem: What should you do with trash?
options: Leave it beside the bin if the recycling station bin is full
Put it in a trash bin or the right recycling container
Pack everything into one bag with no sorting to save space
Collect only paper at home and dump the rest into the same street bin
env_11.explanation: Trash belongs in a bin or the correct recycling container to keep the environment clean and healthy.
theoryLines: Everyone can help keep the environment clean.
Bins are meant for collecting waste.

env_12.stem: How can you help protect nature?
options: Feed wild animals cooked food so visitors can get closer
Do not litter outdoors, and keep natural places clean
Pick rare wild plants to take home as souvenirs
Build trails without protecting sensitive habitats
env_12.explanation: You help nature by not littering, keeping places clean, and respecting plants and animals.
theoryLines: Nature matters for people and for all living things.
Everyone can help protect it.

options: Completely clean air with no pollutants
Harmful materials in the air that damage health and the environment
Rain that always washes every pollutant out of the air
Sunlight that blocks gases from entering the system
env_14.explanation: Air pollution is harmful material in the air from cars, factories, and other sources that can hurt health and nature.
theoryLines: It often comes from human activity.
It can lead to illness.

options: Channel water that is always pure
Adding harmful materials to water that cause damage
A fully clear lake with no microbes
A sweet stream that never carries sediment
env_15.explanation: Water pollution means harmful materials such as waste or chemicals enter water and harm living things that need clean water.
theoryLines: It can hurt nature and people.
Keeping water clean is important.

options: When soil is mixed with fertilizer to help plants grow better.
When harmful materials like chemicals or trash get into the soil and damage living things.
When plants stop growing because the soil is too dry.
When soil is moved from one place to another by wind or water.
env_16.explanation: Soil pollution happens when harmful substances enter the soil and damage the plants, animals, and people who depend on it.
theoryLines: Pollution in the soil affects everything that grows in it.
Chemicals from factories and improperly disposed trash are common sources of soil pollution.

options: When the glass in a real greenhouse breaks and lets cold air inside.
When gases in Earth's atmosphere trap heat from the Sun and warm the planet.
When the Earth is always very cold because the Sun is too far away.
When sunlight simply makes plants grow faster in spring.
env_17.explanation: The greenhouse effect happens when certain gases in the atmosphere trap heat from the Sun, keeping Earth warm enough for life. Too much of this effect can cause the planet to overheat.
theoryLines: Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor trap heat in the atmosphere.
More greenhouse gases mean more heat is trapped, which can warm the planet too much.

options: The weather conditions that change from day to day.
The long-term pattern of weather in a region over many years.
The temperature recorded on just one single day.
The amount of rainfall measured in just one week.
env_18.explanation: Climate is the long-term average of weather conditions in a region. It differs from weather, which describes conditions on a single day.
theoryLines: Climate describes patterns over decades, while weather describes today's conditions.
Different regions have different climates, such as tropical, desert, or polar.

options: Land set aside for continuous city building
A protected area for nature, animals, and plants
A crowded neighborhood with no parks
An industrial site with open waste centers
env_19.explanation: A nature reserve is a protected place where plants and animals are guarded. People may visit carefully without harming wildlife.
theoryLines: Reserves help protect species of animals and plants.
They matter for future generations.

options: Using as many natural resources as possible as fast as you can.
Using resources carefully and responsibly so they are available for future generations.
Only thinking about nature for one special day each year.
Ignoring the environment so that businesses can grow faster.
env_20.explanation: Sustainability means using resources like water, energy, and materials in ways that do not run out or damage the environment, so future generations can meet their own needs too.
theoryLines: Sustainable practices include recycling and using renewable energy sources.
Sustainability protects Earth's resources for future generations.

options: Energy from a limited source that can run out
Energy from sunlight, wind, or water that nature keeps renewing
Energy from swapping limited oil stores
Energy from burning coal
env_21.explanation: Renewable energy comes from sources that do not run out, such as sunlight, wind, and flowing water. It is cleaner than oil and coal.
theoryLines: Renewable energy helps protect the environment.
It is part of living more sustainably.

options: A pile of recycled office paper
Waste from old electronic devices such as computers, phones, and TVs
Empty kitchen plastic bottles
Glass jars from paper recycling
env_22.explanation: Electronic waste comes from old devices. Recycling it matters because it can contain both hazardous and valuable materials.
theoryLines: E-waste is a growing modern problem.
Recycling electronics is important.

env_23.stem: Why is it important to protect the environment?
options: Because pollution always disappears by itself in hours with no action
So nature, animals, and plants can stay healthy
Because there are usually many people in an area
Because there is a place with water
env_23.explanation: Protecting the environment helps keep nature healthy so people can breathe clean air, drink clean water, and live in a cleaner world.
theoryLines: It matters for everyone alive today.
It also matters for future generations.

env_24.stem: What can each person do to protect the environment?
options: Leave lights and air conditioners on standby even when leaving school
Recycle, save water and electricity, and avoid littering outdoors
Buy mostly disposable items to avoid washing dishes
Assume recycling also fixes water pollution with no reduced use
env_24.explanation: People can recycle, save water and electricity, avoid littering, and plant trees and plants.
theoryLines: Every small action helps.
Together, people can make a big difference.

env_14__v2.stem: What is the best way to protect our water sources?
options: Use as much water as you want, since there is always enough.
Avoid dumping waste into water and use water wisely.
Water naturally cleans itself, so no action is needed.
Fill water sources with as many natural materials as possible.
env_14__v2.explanation: Water is a limited resource. When waste, chemicals, or garbage enter rivers, lakes, and oceans, it harms the plants and animals that depend on clean water — including humans. Using water wisely and keeping it clean protects ecosystems and our drinking supply.
theoryLines: Pollution can enter water from factories, farms, and littering.
Clean water is essential for the survival of every living thing on Earth.

options: Putting paper and used oil in the same trash bag with no sorting
Using old materials again to make new things
Leaving unsorted waste in the yard for a long time
Burning mixed yard waste with uncontrolled smoke
env_15__v2.explanation: Recycling means using old materials again to make new products instead of throwing them away.
theoryLines: Recycling helps protect the environment.
It reduces waste and saves resources.

env_16__v2.stem: What helps keep the air clean?
options: Leaving a car engine running in a parking spot when you are not driving
Using cars less and planting trees
Burning yard waste with thick smoke near homes
Assuming strong wind always removes every pollutant forever
env_16__v2.explanation: Using cars less and planting trees helps keep air cleaner.
theoryLines: Clean air is important for health.
Trees help clean the air.

env_17__v2.stem: Which action best helps protect the environment?
options: Burning garbage outdoors to reduce the amount of trash.
Recycling, reducing waste, and avoiding water pollution.
Leaving lights on all night to use less paper.
Increasing factory output to boost production and jobs.
env_17__v2.explanation: Recycling turns used materials into new products instead of sending them to a landfill. Reducing waste means buying and using less in the first place. Keeping chemicals and trash out of water protects ecosystems. Together, these actions lower pollution and conserve natural resources.
theoryLines: The three R's — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle — are a guide to lowering our impact on the environment.
Small everyday choices, like bringing a reusable bag, add up to make a big difference.

options: Air with no particles or gases at all
Harmful materials in the air that hurt health and the environment
Rain that always washes dirt away with no leftovers
Sunlight that blocks gases from entering
env_19__v2.explanation: Air pollution is harmful material in the air from cars, factories, and other sources that can hurt health and nature.
theoryLines: It often comes from human activity.
It can cause illness.

options: Clean water
Adding harmful materials to water that cause damage
Drinking water with no change at all
A pure stream that never touches the ground
env_20__v2.explanation: Water pollution means harmful materials such as waste or chemicals enter water and harm living things that need clean water.
theoryLines: It can hurt nature and people.
Keeping water clean is important.

options: Soil.
Materials to soil.
Soil in not materials.
From not plants.
env_21__v2.explanation: Pollution materials to soil (, ) to plants living.
theoryLines: In soil in the.
On soil.

options: A large city
A set of living things, their habitat, and the links among them
A forest of plants with no animals or water
Wildlife with no plants or food cycles
env_22__v2.explanation: An ecosystem includes living things, their surroundings, and how they interact.
theoryLines: Examples include a forest, a pond, and a coral reef.
A change in the environment can affect every part of the system.

options: A list of all the foods found in one habitat.
A diagram showing how energy flows through many connected food chains in an ecosystem.
A web that spiders build to catch food near plants.
A model that shows only cold-blooded animals and their energy needs.
env_23__v2.explanation: A food web shows how energy moves through an ecosystem by connecting many food chains. It shows how plants, herbivores, and carnivores are all linked.
theoryLines: Plants are the producers at the base of most food webs.
Each part of the food web depends on the other parts.

env_25.stem: What is one good way to help protect the environment?
options: Use as many natural resources as possible each day.
Recycle, save water, and reduce the amount of waste you produce.
Throw all trash away as quickly as possible in large amounts.
Cut down trees to create more open space for buildings.
env_25.explanation: We can protect the environment by making smart daily choices: recycling materials, conserving water, and reducing waste all help reduce our impact on nature.
theoryLines: Small everyday actions like recycling and saving water add up to a big difference.
Everyone can help the environment by being careful about how they use resources.

options: Energy from a limited source that can run out
Energy from sunlight, wind, or water that nature keeps renewing
Energy from swapping limited oil stores
Energy from burning coal
env_26.explanation: Renewable energy comes from sources that do not run out, such as sunlight, wind, and flowing water. It is cleaner than oil and coal.
theoryLines: Renewable energy helps protect the environment.
It is part of living more sustainably.

env_27.stem: Which action best helps reduce waste and protect the environment?
options: Throw all garbage into one trash bag without sorting it
Reuse and recycle materials instead of throwing them away
Dump old materials into rivers or lakes
Buy new products every time instead of repairing old ones
env_27.explanation: Reusing and recycling materials reduces waste and helps protect the environment by keeping harmful items out of landfills and waterways.
theoryLines: Reducing waste keeps the environment clean and healthy.
Recycling turns used materials into new products, saving energy and resources.

env_28.stem: In a big city, more land is covered by concrete and roads, and fewer gardens and trees remain. What is most likely on a hot day?
options: Lower relative humidity in the city center than in a greener area nearby
Higher wind speed only, with no temperature change
More salt in the nearby ocean
All plants in the area stop gas exchange at once
env_28.explanation: Concrete and asphalt heat up and reduce plant evaporation. On hot days this can strengthen the urban heat effect, and relative humidity may drop because there is less plant cooling and shade.
theoryLines: Urban heat islands are linked to ground cover and shade.
Plants cool local areas with shade and water evaporation.

env_29.stem: A farmer overwaters a field with heavy soil. Why might the field produce less food even though more water was added?
options: Long waterlogging can cut off oxygen in the soil, harm roots, and release gases that hurt growth
Water dilutes chlorophyll until it disappears in one day
Plants permanently stop taking in carbon dioxide
Water always makes plants fail because it only carries nitrates
env_29.explanation: Too much water can starve roots of oxygen, hurt nutrient uptake, and lead to root problems. The main issue is not “diluting chlorophyll” or forever stopping carbon dioxide use.
theoryLines: Roots need oxygen for cellular respiration.
Extra water changes oxygen levels in soil and affects soil microbes.

env_30.stem: A crop plant grows very fast after a new farm treatment. Why might that be a warning sign for the ecosystem, not only a success?
options: A fast-spreading crop may crowd out other species and reduce biodiversity
Slow plants are the only ones that harm the environment, so fast growth always means success
Fast growth proves soil and water never need monitoring
Species diversity always rises no matter how land and resources are used
env_30.explanation: A strong competitive advantage can pressure other species and weaken ecological services. Yield in one field is not the whole story.
theoryLines: Biodiversity helps ecosystems stay stable against disease and change.
Changing species relationships can alter a food chain.

env_31.stem: In a lake food web, if the population of small fish crashes suddenly, what is the most likely effect?
options: Larger fish that depend on small fish for food will also decline.
All animals in the lake immediately migrate to a different habitat.
All plants in the lake disappear within days.
The food web stays exactly the same with no changes.
env_31.explanation: In a food web, each species depends on others for food. If small fish disappear, the larger fish, birds, and other animals that eat them lose their main food source. Their populations decline too. This ripple effect is called a trophic cascade.
theoryLines: A food web shows how energy and nutrients flow from producers to consumers in an ecosystem.
When one part of a food web is disrupted, it can affect every other level in the web.

env_32.stem: What is the main difference between recycling paper and reducing paper use from the start?
options: Reducing cuts demand and waste before they happen; recycling deals with waste after it is made
There is no difference; both mean the exact same action
Recycling always uses more energy than making new paper, so it is useless
Reducing only means throwing less away without changing production
env_32.explanation: In the reduce–reuse–recycle order, reducing comes first. Using less paper lowers cutting and manufacturing; recycling helps after products are used.
theoryLines: Reduce comes before reuse, and reuse comes before recycle.
Each step saves resources at a different point in a product’s life.

env_33.stem: Why is a real, lasting rise in greenhouse gases linked to higher average temperatures, not just “more heat from the Sun”?
options: The gases trap more outgoing heat in Earth’s atmosphere and change the energy balance
The Sun’s brightness changes every year exactly like the school calendar
Greenhouse gases absorb all incoming sunlight so day and night disappear
Only the ocean sets temperature, and greenhouse gases only affect gravity
env_33.explanation: Greenhouse gases let in shortwave energy and trap more longwave heat, leading to a warmer balance. The key is stronger heat trapping, not simply “less Sun.”
theoryLines: Earth’s average temperature depends on its energy balance.
Carbon dioxide and methane strengthen the greenhouse effect.

env_34.stem: Why can adding a pesticide without expert guidance also harm species that were not the target, such as fish or helpful insects?
options: Active chemicals can move through a food chain or harm nontarget living things
Pesticides only affect plants and never enter animals
Any natural chemical disappears from the environment in one minute
Only high temperature harms insects
env_34.explanation: Mistakes in use, runoff into water, or different species sensitivity can cause ecological harm. Dose, advice, and careful exposure matter.
theoryLines: Environment and health are linked to careful chemical use.
Different species can be harmed by different amounts of a poison.

env_35.stem: If a new predator fish enters a lake and its population grows quickly, what is the main risk for the lake if nothing balances it?
options: The new predator may wipe out prey and collapse parts of the food web
The predator will always grow forever because food never runs out
All other fish will grow the same amount because competition decreases
The lake will turn into salt water because of the predator alone
env_35.explanation: Without checks, a new predator can drive prey down sharply and threaten ecosystem stability. This is a classic invasive-species risk.
theoryLines: An invasive species can overturn a balance that took years to form.
A stable population depends on flows of energy and matter.

env_36.stem: Why does renewable energy not automatically fix every environmental problem?
options: Turbines, batteries, and mining metals for solar panels still use land and materials
Renewable energy never makes electricity
Wind and sunlight only work at night
Site planning is never needed when something is “natural”
env_36.explanation: Renewables cut fossil-fuel emissions, but they still need infrastructure, materials, and end-of-life handling. A full life-cycle look matters.
theoryLines: Environmental trade-offs include making, running, and retiring equipment.
Building energy sites can still affect habitats.

env_37.stem: In a lake ecosystem, where does most of the energy for all living things originally come from?
options: From the Sun — plants and algae use sunlight through photosynthesis to produce food energy.
From the water — the more water in the lake, the more energy is produced.
From rocks and minerals at the bottom of the lake.
From the oxygen dissolved in the water.
env_37.explanation: In almost every ecosystem, energy comes from the Sun. Plants and algae capture sunlight through photosynthesis and convert it into food. Herbivores eat the plants, carnivores eat the herbivores, and so on — but all that energy originally came from the Sun.
theoryLines: Energy enters the food web through photosynthesis, carried out by plants and algae.
Each step up the food chain uses about 90% of the energy from the step below, so most energy is lost as heat.

env_38.stem: Why can extreme floods increase the wash-off of soil mixed with farm chemicals?
options: Strong runoff can strip topsoil and carry chemicals into drains and streams
Water never touches farm soil
Chemicals stick only to air and never move
Erosion is too rare to change anything in water
env_38.explanation: Heavy rain on bare or packed soil can wash fertilizer and other chemicals into runoff, streams, and reservoirs.
theoryLines: Moving water can carry both soil particles and dissolved chemicals.
Good soil management reduces erosion.

env_39.stem: A child asks why a city beach can feel uncomfortable in summer even when there is little rain. Which science idea best explains both parts?
options: Seasonal climate patterns combine with sea moisture and local urban heat
Weather is identical in every city neighborhood at every moment
The sea releases only salt, so it never affects humidity
Summer always means zero evaporation worldwide
env_39.explanation: Summer can be a drier season for rain, but near the sea there can still be moisture, and concrete plus urban heat can make the air feel hotter and stickier.
theoryLines: Humidity and temperature together shape how hot weather feels.
Seasonal climate and local conditions both matter.

env_40.stem: How can plants along a stream help naturally filter flowing water?
options: Roots and soil structure support mechanical filtering and some chemical uptake
Plants build a concrete barrier that fully blocks water flow
There is no link; only factory filters ever clean water
Flowing water is always clean no matter what plants are nearby
env_40.explanation: Bank plants improve soil structure, reduce erosion, and support microbes that break things down. They help, but they are not a full replacement for treatment systems.
theoryLines: Ecosystem services include natural filtering.
Erosion is closely tied to ground cover.

env_41.stem: If legal fishing drops in a worn-down fishery, but illegal fishing rises, what is the likely result?
options: The fish population may keep falling because total removal stays high
Fish always triple in number no matter the pressure
Only legal fishers affect population size
Illegal fishing instantly increases the size of every male fish
env_41.explanation: Ecological impact depends on total catch in practice. Weak enforcement can undo paper reductions.
theoryLines: Resource management needs rules, monitoring, and community support.
Fishing pressure can change over time.

env_42.stem: Why can building artificial water reservoirs without a water-balance plan harm springs downstream?
options: Pumping groundwater or changing flow can reduce aquifer recharge that feeds springs
Springs always refill themselves with no link to lake water
Artificial reservoirs only increase rainfall, with no pipes involved
Spring water comes only from rain that falls directly on the spring opening
env_42.explanation: Many springs depend on groundwater paths. Poor hydrology planning can cut recharge or change local water pressure.
theoryLines: The water cycle includes surface flow, drainage, and groundwater.
Lakes and water supply projects can change local flow patterns.

env_43.stem: What is the main difference between Earth’s natural greenhouse effect and “the greenhouse effect” in climate-change talks?
options: The natural effect already exists and is needed for life
There is no difference; both terms always mean the same problem
A natural greenhouse means no sunlight reaches Earth
The greenhouse effect happens only in deserts, never over oceans
env_43.explanation: Without natural greenhouse gases, Earth would be too cold for many forms of life. The problem is an extra strengthening of that effect.
theoryLines: Clear science words help us understand problems and solutions.
Earth takes in and gives off radiation in a changing balance.

env_44.stem: Why might reducing nearby farm cottages next to a natural habitat help a rare species — not only mean “less building”?
options: More open space can keep habitat corridors connected and lower the risk of isolation
Any building always increases diversity right away, no matter where it is
Rare species eat only concrete, so more roads are better
Natural habitat never depends on continuous land
env_44.explanation: Connected land supports movement, breeding, and genetic diversity. Habitat fragmentation raises collapse risk.
theoryLines: Landscape planning mixes biology and land-use choices.
Broken-up habitat is a major driver of species loss.

env_45.stem: If a report says temperature trends match human-caused climate change, why must comparisons with older decades be handled carefully?
options: Measurement networks, tools, and geographic coverage have changed over time
Earth never had climate changes in the geologic past
Temperature was never measured before thermometers existed in any way
All past data are usually fake
env_45.explanation: Scientists correct for biases and compare different networks carefully. Method caution is about accuracy, not “doubt for its own sake.”
theoryLines: Data quality and metadata matter in long time-series studies.
Understanding uncertainty is part of scientific learning.

env_46.stem: Why do public gardens often prefer native plants over showy plants that are not suited to the local climate?
options: Native plants often need less watering and care and better support local insects and birds
Native plants always need more outside fertilizer
Native plants never flower, so they are less attractive
There is no ecological difference between native and nonnative plants
env_46.explanation: Climate-matched plants save resources and support local food webs. Nonnative plants can sometimes become invasive.
theoryLines: Living things adapt to local conditions over long periods.
Careful gardening can support city ecosystem services.

env_47.stem: In a lake ecosystem, what single event would cause the most harm to the food web?
options: A pollution event that wipes out the lake's algae and plants.
The lake water becoming slightly cooler in the fall.
Metal objects resting on the bottom of the lake.
The lake having a high concentration of dissolved oxygen.
env_47.explanation: Algae and plants are the producers at the base of the lake's food web. They turn sunlight into food that everything else depends on. If pollution destroys them, all the animals that eat them — and the predators above — lose their food supply, and the whole food web collapses.
theoryLines: Producers, like algae and aquatic plants, form the foundation of every aquatic food web.
Pollution that removes producers causes a chain reaction that affects every organism in the ecosystem.

env_48.stem: Why is changing land use (for example, forest to field) often reported as a strong cause of soil carbon loss?
options: Plants and roots help hold organic carbon in living tissue and soil
Fields always take in more carbon dioxide than forests from day one
Trees contain no carbon at all
Land use only changes map colors and never affects carbon
env_48.explanation: Living plants and soils store carbon. Fast land conversion can release carbon or reduce future uptake.
theoryLines: Forests are important carbon stores.
Land and forest management affect the carbon balance.

env_49.stem: Why does even “soft” nature tourism still need careful planning?
options: Visitor crowds can wear down trails, disturb animals, and bring litter
Soft tourism means no harm is ever possible
Animals never notice noise disturbance
Trash always vanishes by itself in a forest
env_49.explanation: Managing paths, seasons, and visitor behavior reduces ecological pressure. Sustainable tourism is a balance.
theoryLines: Human disturbance is an important conservation factor.
Outdoor learning comes with a duty to act responsibly.

env_50.stem: Why are large animals especially at risk when their habitat shrinks?
options: They need large areas of land to find enough food, water, and space to survive.
Large animals can survive easily without any habitat at all.
Small animals are always more threatened by habitat loss than large ones.
Large animals never need much space to meet their needs.
env_50.explanation: Large animals such as lions, bears, and elephants need vast territories to roam, hunt, and raise their young. When human activity fragments habitats — through roads, farming, or development — these animals cannot find enough food or mates, putting their populations at risk.
theoryLines: Habitat fragmentation is the breaking apart of large natural areas into smaller, disconnected pieces.
When animals cannot travel between habitat patches, populations become isolated and may die out.

env_51.stem: What is true about water quality in a bay after a storm?
options: You need measurements and time — improvement is not always immediate
Water quality always improves instantly with no more testing
A storm always pollutes with no exceptions
Runoff has no link to water quality
env_51.explanation: Storm drains can wash polluted runoff into a bay rather than simply “cleaning” it. Monitoring over time and place matters.
theoryLines: Stormwater management needs hydrology planning.
Measurements let us compare before and after.

env_52.stem: What is one effective way humans can help protect ecosystems from plastic pollution?
options: Use fewer single-use plastic products and dispose of waste properly
Always buy products packaged entirely in plastic
Leave all garbage outdoors so rain can wash it away
Spray chemical fertilizers on plants to help ecosystems recover
env_52.explanation: Using fewer single-use plastics and disposing of waste properly prevents harmful materials from entering ecosystems and harming wildlife.
theoryLines: Plastic pollution harms plants, animals, and waterways in ecosystems.
Choosing safer materials and recycling reduces long-term damage to the environment.

env_53.stem: In an air-pollution agreement between neighboring countries, what must stay consistent so the data can be compared?
options: Shared measurement methods, heights, station locations, and reporting units
Each side can invent its own units with no coordination
Reporting once a year is enough, no matter the wind
Temperature is the only measure that defines air quality
env_53.explanation: Air monitoring depends on protocol: sample height, timing, calibration, and transparency. Without standards, comparisons lose trust.
theoryLines: Good data support public decisions.
Cross-border pollution needs cooperation.
